title: CBSE Class 12 Accountancy · Practice paper 3
subject: Accountancy
label: Practice paper

secNames.A: Accounting for Partnership Firms and Companies

instr: This question paper contains 34 questions. All questions are compulsory.
This question paper is divided into two parts, Part A and Part B.
Part A (Accounting for Partnership Firms and Companies) is compulsory for all candidates.
In the board paper, Part B has two options: (i) Analysis of Financial Statements and (ii) Computerised Accounting. This practice paper gives Option I, Analysis of Financial Statements.
Questions 1 to 16 and 27 to 30 carry 1 mark each.
Questions 17 to 20, 31 and 32 carry 3 marks each.
Questions 23 to 26 and 34 carry 6 marks each. Question 24 is a case-based question with six sub-parts of 1 mark each (multiple choice in the board paper; short answers here).

There is no overall choice. However, an internal choice has been provided in 2 questions of three marks, 2 questions of four marks and 2 questions of six marks (questions 17, 22, 25, 26, 31 and 33). Attempt only one of the alternatives in these questions.
This is a practice paper written in the pattern of the CBSE Sample Question Paper 2026-27. It is not an official CBSE paper.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Anil and Bimal are partners sharing profits and losses in the ratio of 3 : 2. Their fixed capitals are ₹4,00,000 and ₹2,00,000 respectively. The partnership deed allows interest on capital @ 10% p.a., treated as an appropriation of profit. The profit for the year ended 31st March 2026, before interest on capital, was ₹48,000. The interest on capital credited to Anil will be:
questions.sol: Interest due: Anil ₹40,000, Bimal ₹20,000, total ₹60,000. Interest on capital is an appropriation, so it cannot exceed the profit of ₹48,000. The profit is shared in the ratio of interest due (2 : 1): Anil gets 48,000 × 2/3 = ₹32,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
Read the following statements, Assertion (A) and Reason (R), and choose the correct option.
Assertion (A): When a new partner brings his share of goodwill in cash, the amount is credited to the capital accounts of the old partners in their sacrificing ratio.
Reason (R): The sacrificing ratio is always the same as the old profit sharing ratio of the old partners.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is correct explanation to (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not correct explanation of (A).
(A) is false but (R) is correct.
(A) is correct but (R) is false.
questions.sol: (A) is correct: the premium for goodwill compensates the old partners for the share of profit they give up, so it is shared in the sacrificing ratio. (R) is false: the sacrificing ratio equals the old ratio only when nothing else is agreed; if the new partner takes his share in some other proportion, the sacrificing ratio differs from the old ratio.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Arun Ltd. offered 1,00,000 equity shares to the public. Applications were received for 88,000 shares. As per the SEBI guidelines on minimum subscription, the company:
options: can allot 88,000 shares and keep the application money
can allot 88,000 shares only after the next call is paid
must refund the entire application money, as the minimum subscription has not been received
must allot all 1,00,000 shares to the 88,000 applicants
questions.sol: The minimum subscription is 90% of the issue, i.e. 90,000 shares. Applications for only 88,000 shares were received, so no shares can be allotted and the entire application money must be refunded.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: A firm's profits for the years ended 31st March 2024, 2025 and 2026 were ₹90,000, ₹1,20,000 and ₹1,50,000 respectively. The weights assigned to these years are 1, 2 and 3 respectively. The goodwill of the firm at two years' purchase of the weighted average profit will be:

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: X and Y share profits in the ratio of 3 : 2. They decide to share future profits equally. On that date, the Balance Sheet shows Investments at ₹2,50,000 and an Investment Fluctuation Reserve of ₹30,000. The market value of the investments is ₹2,35,000. The amount of Investment Fluctuation Reserve credited to X's Capital Account will be:
questions.sol: Fall in value of investments = 2,50,000 − 2,35,000 = ₹15,000, which is met from the reserve. The balance of ₹15,000 is credited to the partners in the old ratio 3 : 2: X gets 15,000 × 3/5 = ₹9,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: After all adjustments on the admission of C, the capitals of A and B are ₹3,00,000 and ₹1,80,000 respectively. C is admitted for 1/4th share in profits and is to bring capital in proportion to his share, on the basis of the total adjusted capital of A and B. C's capital will be:
questions.sol: A and B together hold 3/4th share with capital ₹4,80,000. Total capital of the new firm = 4,80,000 × 4/3 = ₹6,40,000. C's capital = 6,40,000 × 1/4 = ₹1,60,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: On the admission of a new partner it was found that: (i) investments of ₹10,000 were not recorded in the books; (ii) a creditor of ₹6,000 is not likely to claim the amount and is to be written back; (iii) stock is overvalued by ₹8,000. The result of revaluation will be:
options: Profit ₹12,000
Profit ₹8,000
Loss ₹8,000
Profit ₹24,000
questions.sol: Gains: unrecorded investments ₹10,000 and creditor written back ₹6,000 = ₹16,000. Loss: stock ₹8,000. Profit on revaluation = 16,000 − 8,000 = ₹8,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: A, B and C are partners sharing profits in the ratio of 3 : 2 : 1. B retires. The goodwill of the firm is valued at ₹1,80,000 and A and C decide to share future profits equally. The journal entry for B's share of goodwill will be:
options: A's Capital A/c Dr. ₹45,000 and C's Capital A/c Dr. ₹15,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹60,000
C's Capital A/c Dr. ₹60,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹60,000
A's Capital A/c Dr. ₹30,000 and C's Capital A/c Dr. ₹30,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹60,000
C's Capital A/c Dr. ₹1,80,000; To B's Capital A/c ₹1,80,000
questions.sol: B's share of goodwill = 1,80,000 × 2/6 = ₹60,000. Gain: A = 1/2 − 3/6 = nil; C = 1/2 − 1/6 = 2/6. Only C gains, so C alone compensates B: C's Capital A/c Dr. ₹60,000 To B's Capital A/c ₹60,000.
questions.chapter: Retirement and Death of a Partner

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: D, a partner entitled to 1/4th share of profits, died on 31st December 2025. The firm closes its books on 31st March every year. His share of profit up to the date of death is to be calculated on the basis of the average profit of the last three years, which were ₹1,40,000, ₹1,60,000 and ₹1,80,000. D's share of profit will be:
questions.sol: Average profit = 4,80,000/3 = ₹1,60,000. Profit for 1st April to 31st December 2025 (9 months) = 1,60,000 × 9/12 = ₹1,20,000. D's share = 1,20,000 × 1/4 = ₹30,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: On the dissolution of a firm, the cash balance was ₹20,000 and the other assets realised ₹1,80,000. Creditors of ₹90,000 were paid ₹85,000 in full settlement, realisation expenses were ₹5,000 and a bank loan of ₹30,000 was repaid. The amount available for paying the partners' capitals will be:
questions.sol: Cash available = 20,000 + 1,80,000 = ₹2,00,000. Less creditors ₹85,000, realisation expenses ₹5,000 and bank loan ₹30,000 = ₹1,20,000. Balance for partners' capitals = 2,00,000 − 1,20,000 = ₹80,000.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: When shares issued at par are forfeited, the Share Capital Account is debited with:
options: the amount paid by the shareholder
the nominal (face) value of the shares
the amount called up on the shares
the amount not paid by the shareholder
questions.sol: On forfeiture, the share capital recorded on those shares is cancelled. That is the amount called up, so Share Capital A/c is debited with the called-up amount (the amount paid goes to Share Forfeiture A/c and the unpaid calls are credited).

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: On 1st July 2025, a company issued 5,000, 9% debentures of ₹100 each at par. The interest on these debentures for the year ended 31st March 2026 will be:

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: Discount or loss on issue of debentures is written off in the year in which the debentures are issued:
options: first from Securities Premium (if any), and the balance from the Statement of Profit and Loss
from General Reserve only
from Capital Reserve
only from the Statement of Profit and Loss, in equal instalments over the life of the debentures
questions.sol: Discount or loss on issue of debentures is a capital loss. It is written off in the year of issue, first from the Securities Premium balance (if any) and the balance from the Statement of Profit and Loss.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: A company forfeited 400 equity shares of ₹10 each, fully called up, for non-payment of the first and final call of ₹4 per share. All these shares were reissued at ₹11 per share as fully paid up. The amount transferred to Capital Reserve will be:
questions.sol: Amount forfeited = 400 × (10 − 4) = ₹2,400. The reissue price of ₹11 is above the face value, so no discount is allowed: ₹1 per share (₹400) is credited to Securities Premium, and the whole ₹2,400 forfeited is transferred to Capital Reserve.

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text: On the dissolution of a firm, a loan given to the firm by a partner is paid:
options: before the outside liabilities
after the outside liabilities but before the partners' capitals
after the partners' capitals have been paid
along with the partners' capitals, in the profit sharing ratio
questions.sol: Under Section 48 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, the assets are applied first to pay outside liabilities, then partners' loans (advances), then partners' capitals.

questions.text:
Pass the necessary journal entries in the books of Ajanta Ltd. for the following:
(a) Ajanta Ltd. purchased a building from Mehta Bros. and paid for it in full by issuing 4,000 equity shares of ₹100 each at a premium of 20%.
(b) Ajanta Ltd. took over assets of ₹7,00,000 and liabilities of ₹1,00,000 of Raj Traders for a purchase consideration of ₹5,40,000. The purchase consideration was paid by issuing equity shares of ₹10 each at a premium of ₹2 per share.
Show the calculation of the purchase price of the building in (a) and of the number of shares issued in (b).

(a) Purchase price of the building = 4,000 × ₹120 = ₹4,80,000 (share capital 4,000 × 100 = ₹4,00,000; securities premium 4,000 × 20 = ₹80,000).

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
On 1st April 2025, Pragati Ltd. purchased the business of Mohan Traders, taking over Plant and Machinery of ₹5,00,000, Stock of ₹2,00,000, Debtors of ₹1,40,000 and Creditors of ₹1,20,000, for a purchase consideration of ₹7,60,000. It paid ₹40,000 by cheque and the balance by issuing 10% debentures of ₹100 each at a discount of 10%, redeemable at par.
Interest on the debentures is payable half-yearly on 30th September and 31st March. Before this issue, the company had a balance of ₹5,000 in its Securities Premium Account. The company wrote off the discount on issue of debentures on 31st March 2026. (Ignore tax deducted at source.)

questions.subject: Accountancy
questions.text:
Read the following statements, Assertion (A) and Reason (R), and choose the correct option.
Assertion (A): Issue of equity shares for cash reduces the debt to equity ratio.
Reason (R): Issue of equity shares increases shareholders' funds, while long-term debt remains unchanged.
options: Both A and R are correct, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is correct but R is incorrect
A is incorrect but R is correct
questions.sol: Debt to equity ratio = Long-term debt ÷ Shareholders' funds. Issuing shares increases shareholders' funds without changing debt, so the ratio falls. A and R are both correct and R explains A.

(i) Gross profit = 20,00,000 − 12,00,000 = ₹8,00,000. Gross Profit Ratio = 8,00,000/20,00,000 × 100 = 40%.
(ii) Operating cost = 12,00,000 + 3,00,000 = ₹15,00,000. Operating Ratio = 15,00,000/20,00,000 × 100 = 75%.
(iii) Net profit before interest and tax = 8,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹5,00,000; profit before tax = 5,00,000 − 1,00,000 = ₹4,00,000; profit after tax = 4,00,000 − 1,60,000 = ₹2,40,000. Net Profit Ratio = 2,40,000/20,00,000 × 100 = 12%.
(iv) Capital employed = 10,00,000 + 5,00,000 + 10,00,000 = ₹25,00,000. Return on Investment = Net profit before interest and tax/Capital employed × 100 = 5,00,000/25,00,000 × 100 = 20%.

points.t: (i) Gross Profit Ratio 40%
(ii) Operating Ratio 75%
(iii) Net Profit Ratio 12% (profit after tax ₹2,40,000)
(iv) Return on Investment 20% (₹5,00,000 ÷ ₹25,00,000)

or.text:
The current ratio of Rohit Ltd. is 2.5 : 1 and its quick ratio is 1.5 : 1. Its working capital is ₹3,00,000. Its current assets consist only of quick assets and inventory. Calculate:
(i) Current liabilities
(ii) Current assets
(iii) Quick assets
(iv) Inventory
or.model:
(i) Let current liabilities = x. Current assets = 2.5x. Working capital = 2.5x − x = 1.5x = 3,00,000, so x = ₹2,00,000.
(ii) Current assets = 2.5 × 2,00,000 = ₹5,00,000.
(iii) Quick assets = 1.5 × 2,00,000 = ₹3,00,000.
(iv) Inventory = Current assets − Quick assets = 5,00,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹2,00,000.

points.t: (i) Current liabilities ₹2,00,000 (1.5 × CL = ₹3,00,000)
(ii) Current assets ₹5,00,000
(iii) Quick assets ₹3,00,000
(iv) Inventory ₹2,00,000
